svg.title: The five layers of multicast QoS as a chain, and the four reasons multicast makes them harder than unicast
svg.desc: A five-stage chain across the top. One, classification and marking, where multicast usually inherits the source's DSCP which is often zero, so the network edge must re-mark. Two, ingress trust, where access ports either trust DSCP or re-mark with a policy map, and uncontrollable terminals are never trusted. Three, queuing, where multicast goes into a dedicated bandwidth queue rather than LLQ, because putting video into LLQ starves signalling. Four, congestion management, where queue length and WRED must be tuned for UDP, since too long adds jitter and too short drops. Five, shaping and policing at the source and at domain edges to stop one source saturating a link. Below, the four difficulties: aggregated traffic that cannot be limited per session, no reverse feedback, replication in the middle that amplifies congestion, and layer 2 flooding that breaks the QoS assumptions before any queue can help. A footer notes that the chain fails at its weakest link, and the weakest link is usually the access layer without snooping.
svg.text: Multicast QoS is a chain of five stages, and it breaks at the weakest one
Marking at the edge is worthless if the access layer floods, and a perfect queue cannot save a link that was already saturated upstream.
the sender never marked it, so the
edge must - and nothing else will
trust dscp where the terminal is
controlled, re-mark where it is not
trusting a PC is a policy hole
any host can then claim EF and
win the queue against real video
priority queue eats the control plane
so drops are simply lost frames
policer at the source, shaper at
one source can saturate a link
WHY IT IS HARDER THAN UNICAST
one link carries hundreds of groups;
there is no "per session" to rate limit,
so capacity is the only unit of control
What you configure is what it sends
by the topology, not by the sender
without snooping the access link is
saturated at line rate, and no queue
can recover a link already full

Rule for the design document: name the weakest hop explicitly. "QoS is configured" means nothing; "the access switch has snooping, the uplink has a 30 percent queue, the encoder is policed at 20 Mbps" is a design.
End-to-end means end to end: one unclassified hop, one hop without a queue, or one VLAN without snooping, and the service behaves as if no QoS was designed at all.
Testing note: verify with a burst, not with a steady stream. Steady-state tests pass on links that drop badly during the I-frame bursts of real video.
Collect interface output drops, per-queue drops and the receiver's own loss counter - the first two can look clean while the third climbs.
